_about.purpose: Labelled retrieval set for calibrating Embedder.vector_ceiling.
_about.why: Week 8 set the ceiling to 0.75 from nine tariff lines. Nine is enough to show that 0.55 was wrong and not enough to show that 0.75 is right. A threshold is a claim about the separation between what the corpus can answer and what it cannot, and that claim needs labelled negatives.
_about.shape: A corpus of published tariff text, ten queries the corpus does answer, and ten it does not. The negatives are the load-bearing half: any ceiling retrieves the positives if it is loose enough, and vector search always returns something.
_about.embedded_text: '{code} {description_en}' — identical to scripts/embed_corpus.py, so a benchmark distance is the same number production would see.
_about.negatives_are_absent_goods_not_adjacent_: A hard negative here is a good the corpus does not carry, phrased like one it does. Deliberately NOT an adjacent 8-digit subheading of a line that is present: 8482.10 ball bearings and 8482.20 roller bearings are semantically near-identical, and no distance threshold separates them. That case is real, and it is handled by TariffHit.needs_analyst_confirmation rather than by a ceiling. Asserting a threshold could do it would be asserting something false.
_about.expects_vs_expects_hs6: `expects` is the exact line in THIS fixture's 24-line corpus, which is what tests/integration/test_tariff_benchmark.py measures against. `expects_hs6` is the six-digit subheading, and it is what scripts/calibrate_thresholds.py measures against the published schedule. The two differ because the real HTSA subdivides each subheading into statistical suffixes that a goods description cannot determine: 0901.21 splits eight ways on organic certification, Arabica versus Robusta, and container size, none of which appears in 'roasted cofee beans, not decafinated'. Scoring a plain-language query against a ten-digit code would be scoring the model on facts the query does not contain. Six digits is the level a description supports, and it is also the level that is harmonised internationally, which is why tariff_lines.hs6 exists as the cross-jurisdiction join key.
_about.negatives_against_the_full_schedule: Nine of the ten negatives below are negatives only relative to this fixture's 24-line corpus. Live cattle, cut roses, raw sugar, printed books and wooden pencils are all real headings in the published HTSA, so against the full schedule they are positives whose answer was never recorded here. Only 'marine cargo insurance brokerage' stays a negative at any volume, because it is not a good. scripts/calibrate_thresholds.py scores that one and says plainly that it is ignoring the rest; counting them would measure this fixture going stale and report it as precision.
_about.week_17_expansion: Week 16 reported 4/10 against 3/10 at rank one and had to add that one query is not a difference. Fifty positives is what it takes for a single query to stop being worth 10 percentage points. The forty added here were resolved out of data/hts_2026_full.json rather than written from memory: `expects` is a subheading that exists in the published schedule and `description_en` is that subheading's resolved ancestor chain, so a fixture distance stays comparable to a production one. They are labelled at the subheading rather than the statistical suffix for the reason `expects_vs_expects_hs6` already gives - a goods description does not determine a suffix, and labelling one would be labelling a coin toss.
_about.negatives_are_now_flagged: `survives_full_schedule` replaces the hardcoded string in calibrate_thresholds.py. Nine of the original ten negatives are goods the 24-line corpus lacks and the published schedule carries, so against the full HTSA they are positives with no recorded answer. Five services were added because that is the shape of negative that survives any corpus: a customs brokerage fee is not a good, and no number of tariff lines makes it one.
